metadata.title: Grounding & Communication Foundations — Sources
metadata.description: Primary references for 10 grounding-theory primitives: common ground, grounding criterion, contributions (presentation+acceptance), evidence of understanding, repair, presupposition, audience design, joint commitment, least collaborative effort, grounding cost. Clark canonical layer plus modern multi-agent LLM application.

canonical_texts.name: Grounding in Communication
canonical_texts.description: Clark and Brennan (1991). In Resnick, Levine, & Teasley (eds.) Perspectives on Socially Shared Cognition (APA). Canonical paper introducing grounding criterion, evidence of understanding hierarchy, and grounding cost across communication tracks. Primary source for primitives #1, #2, #4, #10.

canonical_texts.name: Using Language
canonical_texts.description: Clark (1996). Cambridge University Press. Book-length treatment of language as joint action; covers contributions, joint commitment, and least collaborative effort. Primary source for primitives #3, #8, #9.

canonical_texts.name: Contributing to Discourse
canonical_texts.description: Clark and Schaefer (1989). Cognitive Science 13(2):259–294. Defines presentation and acceptance phases of contributions. Primary source for primitive #3.

canonical_texts.name: Referring as a Collaborative Process
canonical_texts.description: Clark and Wilkes-Gibbs (1986). Cognition 22(1):1–39. Establishes least collaborative effort principle through referring expressions. Primary source for primitive #9.

canonical_texts.name: The Preference for Self-Correction in the Organization of Repair in Conversation
canonical_texts.description: Schegloff, Jefferson, and Sacks (1977). Language 53(2):361–382. Foundational conversation-analysis paper on repair sequences. Primary source for primitive #5.

canonical_texts.name: Logic and Conversation
canonical_texts.description: Grice (1975). In Cole and Morgan (eds.) Syntax and Semantics 3: Speech Acts. Cooperative principle, conversational implicature, foundation for presupposition theory. Primary source for primitive #6.

canonical_texts.name: Pragmatic Presuppositions
canonical_texts.description: Stalnaker (1974). In Munitz and Unger (eds.) Semantics and Philosophy. Formal account of presupposition as common-ground requirement. Primary source for primitive #6.

canonical_texts.name: Language Style as Audience Design
canonical_texts.description: Bell (1984). Language in Society 13(2):145–204. Audience design framework. Primary source for primitive #7.

canonical_texts.name: Audience Design in Meaning and Reference
canonical_texts.description: Clark and Murphy (1982). In Le Ny and Kintsch (eds.) Language and Comprehension. Tailoring of meaning to audience. Secondary source for primitive #7.

canonical_texts.name: Agreeing to Disagree
canonical_texts.description: Aumann (1976). Annals of Statistics 4(6):1236–1239. Formal common-knowledge result; mutual-belief mathematics underlying common ground. Primary source for primitive #1 formal layer.

canonical_texts.name: Convention: A Philosophical Study
canonical_texts.description: Lewis (1969). Harvard University Press / Blackwell. Common knowledge as basis for convention and coordination. Foundational source for primitive #1.

canonical_texts.name: Relevance: Communication and Cognition
canonical_texts.description: Sperber and Wilson (1986/1995). Blackwell. Relevance theory; alternative framework to Gricean implicature. Secondary source for primitives #6, #7.

canonical_texts.name: Conceptual Pacts and Lexical Choice in Conversation
canonical_texts.description: Brennan and Clark (1996). Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 22(6):1482–1493. Conceptual pacts as personal common ground. Secondary source for primitives #1, #7.

canonical_texts.name: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
canonical_texts.description: Cemri et al. (2025). NeurIPS. Empirical taxonomy of 14 multi-agent LLM failure modes across 1,600+ traces, grouped into system design issues, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. Primary modern source for connecting grounding theory to LLM agent failures.

canonical_texts.name: A Computational Theory of Grounding in Natural Language Conversation
canonical_texts.description: Traum (1994). PhD thesis, University of Rochester. Computational implementation of grounding for dialogue systems; bridge between Clark's framework and computational agents. Secondary source for all primitives in computational application.

canonical_texts.name: Navigating Rifts in Human-LLM Grounding: Study and Benchmark
canonical_texts.description: Shaikh, Mozannar, Bansal, Fourney, Horvitz (2025). ACL 2025. Taxonomy of grounding acts; Rifts benchmark from WildChat, MultiWOZ, Bing Chat logs showing LLMs initiate clarification 3x less and follow-up 16x less than humans; early grounding failures predict later breakdown. Primary evidence for #4, #5.

canonical_texts.name: NewsInterview: a Dataset and a Playground to Evaluate LLMs' Grounding Gap via Informational Interviews
canonical_texts.description: Spangher, Lu, Kalyan, Cho, Huang, Shi, May (2025). ACL 2025. 45,848 NPR/CNN interviews; human interviewers produce acknowledgements in ~9% of utterances, all LLM variants produce ~0%; LLMs also fail at audience-state-sensitive pivoting. Supports #4, #7.

canonical_texts.name: Understanding Common Ground Misalignment in Goal-Oriented Dialog: A Case-Study with Ubuntu Chat Logs
canonical_texts.description: Sarkar, Srikanth, Pellegrin, Rudinger, Bonial, Resnik (2025). ACL 2025. 200 dyadic Ubuntu IRC conversations (7,590 turns); operationalizes Clark & Brennan common ground as conversational friction; friction correlates with task failure; GPT-4o detects overt friction at 77.22% F1, implicit at 64.81%. Supports #1, #5.

canonical_texts.name: Preemptive Detection and Correction of Misaligned Actions in LLM Agents
canonical_texts.description: Fang, Zhu, Gurevych (2025). EMNLP 2025. InferAct: two-unit system (Task Inference + Task Verification) detects misalignment before irreversible action; best Macro-F1 in 11/12 settings across 3 tasks × 4 LLMs, +8% avg over strongest baseline. Extends primitive #5 with preemptive repair pattern.

canonical_texts.name: Collaborative Rational Speech Act: Pragmatic Reasoning for Multi-Turn Dialog
canonical_texts.description: Estienne, Ben Zenou, Naderi, Cheung, Piantanida (2025). EMNLP 2025. CRSA: information-theoretic RSA extension with private meaning spaces, dialogue-history-conditioned gain function, and belief tracking. Outperforms RSA baseline; speaker entropy 8.18 vs 14.27 (RSA) on MDDial. Grounds #8, #9.

canonical_texts.name: Grounding Gaps in Language Model Generations
canonical_texts.description: Shaikh, Gligorić, Khetan, Gerstgrasser, Yang, Jurafsky (2024). NAACL-HLT 2024. Coins 'presumptive grounders': LLMs assume common ground rather than using grounding acts (clarification, acknowledgment). Introduces grounding-act taxonomy and metrics. Key finding: RLHF/preference training reduces grounding acts. Predecessor to Rifts ACL 2025 (same first author). Code+benchmarks: github.com/oshaikh13/grounding-gaps. Evidence grade B. Primary evidence for #4, #5.

canonical_texts.name: The FACTS Grounding Leaderboard: Benchmarking LLMs' Ability to Ground Responses to Long-Form Input
canonical_texts.description: Jacovi et al. (2025). Google. arXiv 2501.03200, January 2025. Leaderboard benchmarking LLMs' factual grounding to long-form documents (up to 32K tokens). 1,719 examples (860 public, 859 private). RAG-attribution sense of grounding: whether generated responses remain grounded in provided documents. Scope: LLM-attribution grounding only — distinct from Clark conversational grounding covered by this skill's primitives.

canonical_texts.name: RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
canonical_texts.description: Es, James, Espinosa Anke, Schockaert (2024). EACL 2024. Framework for evaluating RAG systems without ground-truth annotations. Faithfulness metric operationalizes claim→source grounding for RAG pipelines. Scope: RAG-attribution grounding only — distinct from Clark conversational grounding covered by this skill's primitives.

canonical_texts.name: Correctness is not Faithfulness in RAG Attributions
canonical_texts.description: Wallat, Heuss, de Rijke, Anand (2024). arXiv 2412.18004, December 2024; ICTIR 2025. Distinguishes correctness (cited documents support statements) from faithfulness (model genuinely relies on cited documents). Up to 57% of citations are post-rationalized — correct in appearance but not genuinely grounded in the source. Evidence grade A. Scope: RAG-attribution grounding only — distinct from Clark conversational grounding covered by this skill's primitives.

canonical_texts.name: GSAR: Typed Grounding for Hallucination Detection and Recovery in Multi-Agent LLMs
canonical_texts.description: Kamelhar (2026). arXiv 2604.23366, April 2026. PREPRINT — no peer review confirmed; code not confirmed in public repo. Applies Clark-vocabulary grounding to multi-agent output verification. Four-way claim typology: grounded, ungrounded, contradicted, complementary. Evidence-type-specific weights, asymmetric contradiction-penalised score, three-tier decision function (proceed/regenerate/replan) under compute budget. Evaluated on FEVER. Maps to Primitive #5 (Repair) and #4 (Evidence of Understanding).

canonical_texts.name: Learning to Ask: When LLM Agents Meet Unclear Instruction
canonical_texts.description: Wang et al. (2025). EMNLP 2025, pp. 21773–21784. NoisyToolBench: ambiguous real-world tool-use instructions. Ask-when-Needed (AwN) framework: agents ask clarifying questions when encountering unclear instruction obstacles. Significantly outperforms existing frameworks on NoisyToolBench. Operationalizes Primitive #5 (Repair) — ask-for-clarification channel — in tool-use agent context. Complements InferAct (preemptive) with ambiguity-triggered reactive clarification. Code+datasets released. Evidence grade B.

canonical_texts.name: Talk is Cheap, Communication is Hard: Dynamic Grounding Failures and Repair in Multi-Agent Negotiation
canonical_texts.description: Yao, Zou, Hawkins (2026). arXiv 2605.01750v2, May 2026. PREPRINT — no peer review confirmed. Introduces the static-vs-dynamic grounding distinction: static maps language to shared context, dynamic requires negotiating meaning across turns. Iterated multi-turn negotiation game where two agents allocate shared resources to private projects with verifiable jointly optimal outcomes. Key result: agents identify Pareto-optimal allocations in isolation but dyads consistently fail to reach them across models — the coordination gap is not explained by individual reasoning limits or insufficient information exchange. Four failure modes: loss of shared interaction history (#1), stubborn anchoring to early proposals (#3, #8), defaulting to equal splits over reward-maximizing coordination (#2), referential binding errors across turns (#6). Grounds the multi-turn agent-agent coordination recipe.

canonical_texts.name: A Benchmark to Assess Common Ground in Human-AI Collaboration
canonical_texts.description: Poelitz, Doshi-Velez, Lindley (2026). arXiv 2602.21337v1, February 2026. PREPRINT — no peer review confirmed. Helper/Worker collaborative puzzle-matching task; 40 Prolific participants in a 2x2 design (role x shared/non-shared view), four trials plus practice. Measures common ground at three levels: task (success, word and turn counts), object (shared referential conventions), communication (presentations, clarifications, repairs, acceptances). Key findings: shared visual feedback raises accuracy (chi-sq(1)=11.57, p<0.001); no learning effect across trials for AI, contrary to human-human patterns; human Helpers reduce communication over trials (F(1,28)=11.67, p<0.01) while AI Helpers show minimal efficiency gain; joint vocabulary stays small and shrinks (F(1,28)=12.28, p<0.001); models fail to update assumptions after repairs. Small sample — treat effect directions as informative, magnitudes as provisional. Supports #1, #4, #5.

canonical_texts.name: Beyond Message Passing: A Semantic View of Agent Communication Protocols
canonical_texts.description: Yuan, Lyu, Yuan, Zhang, He, Geng, Du, Sun, Chen, Han, Kang, Chen, Wu, Liu (2026). arXiv 2604.02369v3, submitted March 2026, revised April 2026. PREPRINT — no peer review confirmed. Surveys 18 representative agent communication protocols (MCP, A2A, Agent Protocol, Agora, ACP variants) against a three-layer taxonomy: communication (reliable transmission), syntactic (message schemas), semantic (meaning alignment). Invokes Clark's joint-activity framing — communication requires mutual belief about shared knowledge, intentions, assumptions — to motivate the semantic layer. Key finding: most protocols provide limited protocol-level mechanisms for clarification, context alignment, and verification; semantic responsibilities are pushed into prompts, wrappers, and application-specific orchestration logic. Agents 'exchange messages correctly without ensuring they understand them in the same way.' Citable support for the A2A/MCP transport-vs-grounding boundary. Supports #3, #5, #6.

canonical_texts.name: NC-Bench: An LLM Benchmark for Evaluating Conversational Competence
canonical_texts.description: Moore, An, Ahmed, Gala (2026). arXiv 2601.06426v2, March 2026. PREPRINT — no peer review confirmed. Conversation-analysis-grounded benchmark measuring the form and structure of natural conversation rather than content accuracy. 14 interaction patterns across three sets (basic, RAG, complex request); 720 test cases (180/180/360); 6 open-source models from 3 families (Granite, Llama, Qwen) at 2-8B. Key result for this skill: repair is the weakest competence class — 5-75% accuracy on repeat requests against 95-100% on answering inquiries; sequence closers 55-100%; sequence abort 20-100%. Small-model sample: the absolute rates do not transfer to frontier models, but the ordering (repair weakest, answering strongest) is the usable finding. Supports #5.
